description: Computer Science, cybersecurity and problem solving geeks. We're taking on Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots, to help build a clear, evidence-based tool from NASA data!
summary:
We developed SHARP (Satellite Harmonization and Activity Records Platform), a web application for exploring burning activity through NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations.

These sensors detect hotspots at different resolutions and observation times, making their raw counts difficult to compare. SHARP groups afternoon observations on a shared 2 km grid and calibrates MODIS Aqua activity against VIIRS using overlapping reporting periods. Users can select a country or draw an area of interest, explore a burning activity calendar, inspect individual observations, and export data. Historical comparisons show seasonal patterns and differences between periods where reporting coverage is available.

SHARP connects the harmonization method to the records behind each result. Researchers and land managers can examine regional burning patterns, check data sources and coverage gaps, and assess how recent activity compares with the available historical record. This supports more informed monitoring while keeping the limits of satellite observations visible.
details:
What we built

SHARP, the Satellite Harmonization and Activity Records Platform, is a web application for investigating burning activity using NASA FIRMS observations from MODIS and VIIRS.

Users can explore recent hotspots on an interactive globe, select a country or draw an area of interest, and examine the observations within that boundary. The analysis workspace connects a burning activity calendar with satellite comparisons, detection records, historical views and downloadable results.

The project addresses a central difficulty in the challenge: MODIS and VIIRS observe the Earth with different resolutions, sensitivities and observation schedules. Their raw detection counts require careful treatment before they can support comparisons across time.

How the harmonization works

Our harmonized activity metric uses MODIS aboard Aqua together with selected VIIRS platforms. These platforms belong to the afternoon orbit group, which reduces one source of difference caused by observation timing.

The backend assigns hotspot coordinates to a shared equal-area grid with nominal 2 km spacing. Multiple observations within the same cell on the same UTC day contribute one occupied cell to the relevant sensor group.

For periods with VIIRS reporting, the metric uses the union of occupied cells from the selected VIIRS platforms. Aqua observations are kept separate from that total. For earlier Aqua periods, the backend can scale Aqua’s occupied-cell counts using the median daily VIIRS-to-Aqua ratio from overlapping reporting periods. This requires at least 14 qualifying overlap days.

The resulting values describe daily occupied cells. Monthly totals describe active-cell-days. Original detection records remain available for inspection alongside the aggregated results.

Exploring an area

Users can select a country with its geographic boundary or draw a custom area. They can then:

  • Choose a date range and examine daily activity.
  • Compare MODIS and VIIRS observations.
  • Filter records by supported satellite, confidence, day/night and fire radiative power criteria.
  • Inspect acquisition times and source information.
  • Explore monthly and seasonal patterns where historical reporting is available.
  • Export records as CSV, GeoJSON or JSON.
  • Capture a map for further analysis or presentation.

Benefits and intended impact

SHARP is intended for researchers, land managers and emergency-management teams investigating regional burning patterns. It brings the map, calendar, records and method information into one workflow.

A user can examine when reported activity increased, compare periods with adequate historical coverage, and inspect the observations behind a result. This can support seasonal monitoring, investigation of unusual activity and planning for periods that warrant closer attention.

Historical analysis depends on the data loaded for the selected region. We distinguish the availability of a historical processing pipeline from the availability of a complete historical record.

What makes the approach distinctive

We connected the harmonization method to the interface where users interpret its results. The calendar and historical views sit alongside source records, coverage information and calibration evidence.

The shared grid provides a consistent aggregation unit, while the overlap-based scaling makes the cross-sensor adjustment explicit. Users can inspect the supporting observations and understand how a value was produced.

We also separated worldwide visualization from detailed regional investigation. The global map uses cached raster hotspot tiles, while the analysis tools handle record inspection and exports. Shared backend ingestion and storage allow visitors to reuse the same acquired observations.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, HTML and CSS.
  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Mantine and Radix/shadcn-style interface components.
  • Mapping and geometry: MapLibre GL JS, Terra Draw and geospatial geometry utilities.
  • Backend: FastAPI, Uvicorn and HTTPX.
  • Storage: SQLite for shared observations, caching and historical workflows.
  • Data: NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS products, with NASA GIBS imagery and geographic reference layers.
  • Development: Git, GitHub, ESLint, Prettier and automated frontend and backend tests.

Factors we considered

We considered sensor differences, observation timing, repeated detections, reporting completeness, geographic boundaries and the limits of historical coverage. We also considered loading performance, shared API usage, mobile layouts, keyboard interaction, readable colors and source attribution.

The analysis represents satellite-reported hotspot activity. Its calibration depends on the available regional overlap, and agreement measured on those fitting days is not independent validation. These limits matter when interpreting trends and comparing periods.
